title: Algorithmic Problem Solving: Longest Common Prefix String Scanning
concepts_and_definitions: Longest Common Prefix (LCP) – the longest string that is a prefix of all strings in a set
Binary Search – divide‑and‑conquer technique to find a boundary in a sorted or monotonic space
HashSet – collection that stores unique elements, used to count character occurrences
String Scanning – iterating over characters of strings to compare prefixes
Time Complexity – analysis of algorithmic steps relative to input size
Space Complexity – amount of memory used by an algorithm
mechanisms_and_formulas: Binary search update rules: low = mid + 1 if prefix common, high = mid - 1 otherwise
Prefix check: all strings share same character at position i → prefix length i+1 is common
HashMap counting: if count of a character equals number of strings, it is common at that position
Time complexity of linear scan LCP: O(n * m) where n is number of strings and m is min length
examples_and_code_patterns: Java loop for LCP: for (int i=0; i<minLen; i++) { char c = strs[0].charAt(i); for (int j=1; j<strs.length; j++) if (strs[j].charAt(i)!=c) return sb.toString(); sb.append(c); }
HashSet approach: for each position, add character to set; if set size >1 break;
Binary search LCP: while (low <= high) { mid = (low+high)/2; if (isCommonPrefix(mid)) { result=mid; low=mid+1; } else high=mid-1; }
Cocoa eating bananas example: binary search on speed to find minimal hours <= H
factual_summary_text: The session reviewed two algorithmic problems: the Longest Common Prefix (LCP) and the Cocoa Eating Bananas problem. For LCP, students examined a straightforward linear scan that compares characters position by position across all strings, stopping when a mismatch occurs. The class also explored a HashSet-based method that counts character occurrences at each position to determine commonality, and a binary search strategy that treats the prefix length as a search space, halving the interval based on whether a candidate length is valid. Discussions highlighted Java memory management nuances, such as object allocation, reference handling, and garbage collection, contrasting them with C++’s explicit delete/free semantics. The Cocoa Eating Bananas problem was introduced as a classic binary search application: given piles of bananas and a time limit, the goal is to find the minimal eating speed that allows all bananas to be consumed within the allotted hours. Students practiced brute‑force enumeration of speeds and then moved to a binary search over speed values, computing the total hours needed for each candidate speed. Throughout, the instructor emphasized clean code practices, the importance of breaking loops correctly, and the need to clear data structures between iterations to avoid stale counts.
